questions.why: False. Only 28.9% reached 3R, and 20.4% reached 5R, so most didn't. That's normal for a good setup. You win by keeping the losses small on the ones that fail and letting the few that run, run. That's why the stop matters so much. A past rate isn't a promise for the next trade either.
questions.lesson_line: Most won't run. The ones that do pay for the rest.

reasons: our own scan's base rate, read from our bars (survivors only), not yet reviewed by the owner
replaces the cut q64 without the web quotes

deeper.trap: Reading a past rate as a promise. A base rate says how often it happened in past scan hits, not how the next trade ends.

questions.q: You can hold a trade through earnings once it's up 3R.
questions.simple: False. The bar is 5R, so a bad gap on the report still leaves you with a winner.
questions.why: False. We hold through a report only when the trade's up 5R. A report can gap the stock right through your stop overnight. At 5R up, you've got enough cushion that a bad gap still leaves you with a winner. At 3R, one bad gap can wipe it out. Under 5R going into the report, sell before it.
questions.lesson_line: Hold through a report only if you're up 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's earnings rule (B22)

questions.q: By our card, what does the size of this gap do to the trade?
questions.story: A leader's earnings gap closes the day 38% above the prior close. Weeks later it tests the gap-up low and closes near its high. Every other check on the card passes.
choices: It lowers the grade, but not a ban
It bans it; over 30% is never bought
It raises the grade; demand is strong
It does not count; only the test does
questions.answer: It lowers the grade, but not a ban
questions.why: It lowers the grade, but it is not a ban. On our card, a gap over 30% is a lower grade, not a ban. Wagner warns that an opening gap of more than 30% could lead to a few months of chop.
questions.lesson_line: On our card, a gap over 30% lowers the grade but does not ban the trade.

wrong.It bans it; over 30% is never bought: Our card makes a gap over 30% a lower grade, not a ban.
wrong.It raises the grade; demand is strong: It is the reverse. A gap over 30% grades lower, and Wagner warns of months of chop.
wrong.It does not count; only the test does: The gap size is part of the grade on our card, even with a clean test.

questions.simple: On our card a gap over 30 percent lowers the grade, but the trade is not banned.

reasons: proposed 30% line on the card, not yet ruled by the owner
one web source (Wagner), already checked on the page

questions.q: A friend always puts the stop 1% under the line. What's the problem with that here?
questions.story: The last bar is the test day. Its low dips 1.8% under the gap-up low. Then it closes back over the line at 87% of its range.
choices: Today's low is already below it
It's too far away from your entry
The stop belongs on the line
questions.answer: Today's low is already below it
questions.why: Today's low is already below it. The low went 1.8% under the line. A stop 1% under would've been hit today, in a day that ended up holding. A fixed cushion ignores what the stock actually did. Slight breaches often go deeper than that. Put the stop a few cents under the test day's real low, the low of the day. That's the price that proves the hold failed.
questions.lesson_line: The day's real low sets the stop, not a fixed cushion.

wrong.It's too far away from your entry: It's the reverse. A 1% stop sits above this day's low, inside its range.
wrong.The stop belongs on the line: The stop goes a few cents under the test day's low, not on the line.
wrong.No undercut is ever allowed: Slight undercuts are fine, even good. Some of the best tests break the line and snap back.

questions.simple: Today already traded below that stop. Put it a few cents under the test day's real low instead.

reasons: proposed criterion on the card (gs.stop_not_porosity), not yet ruled by the owner
the 3.2% dip is given in the story and sits inside the card's up-to-5% undercut allowance

deeper.counter: Gil Morales and Chris Kacher allow a 1 to 2% undercut of the gap-up low in some cases. This test went 1.8% under and closed at 87% of its range.

questions.q: You check the 200-day on the test day's close, not the gap day's.
questions.why: True. What matters is where the stock is when you buy. A gap day above the 200-day can fade back under it by the time the test comes. If the test day closes under the 200, it's off. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks, full stop.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 200-day on the test day's close.
questions.simple: True. The test day is when you buy, so that's the close that has to be over the 200-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's 200-day rule (B26)

questions.q: You bought this test and it's working. When can your stop come up to breakeven?
choices: From 2R to 5R, or at a first sell
The moment your buy order is filled
Only after your very last sell
questions.answer: From 2R to 5R, or at a first sell
questions.why: Somewhere between 2R and 5R, or when you make your first sell. Breakeven means the stop goes up to your buy price, so a winner can't turn into a loser. Do it too early, at 1R, and normal wiggle stops you out of a good trade for nothing. Wait until it's up 2R to 5R and the trade has proved itself. Where in that window is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Let it prove itself, then lock in breakeven.

wrong.The moment your buy order is filled: Way too early. At the fill, the stop stays under the test day's low.
wrong.As soon as it's up 1R: Too soon. At 1R normal wiggle takes you out. Wait for 2R to 5R.
wrong.Only after your very last sell: Too late. By then there's nothing left to protect.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell. Any sooner and normal wiggle stops you out for nothing.
